title: FDA raises smoked salmon recall to its highest risk level over listeria
excerpt: The FDA has upgraded two Starfish Seafood smoked salmon recalls to Class I — its highest risk level — over possible listeria contamination. Check the best-before dates before serving any smoked salmon at home.
content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has upgraded two ongoing smoked seafood recalls to its highest risk classification over concerns about possible Listeria monocytogenes contamination.

Both recalls, involving Starfish Seafood products, were officially classified as Class I on November 3, 2026. A Class I designation means consuming the affected products could cause serious health consequences or even death, according to the FDA.

The recalls were first issued voluntarily on October 6 by Krasnyi Oktyabr Inc., a Brooklyn-based wholesale distributor, after testing by the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets identified possible listeria contamination.

Which products are affected

  • Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Norwegian Salmon, sliced — best-before date November 27, 2027
  • Starfish Seafood Cold Smoked Trio — Salmon, Halibut, Trout

Both products originated in Latvia, and 86 cases of each were recalled, according to the FDA's enforcement reports. The affected products were distributed in nine states. Webb Watch 956 could not confirm from the published reports whether any of the recalled product reached Texas stores — check the product name and best-before date, and do not eat it if it matches.

The distributor told Newsweek that trace amounts of bacteria were found on plastic packaging that had come into contact with the seafood, rather than in the seafood itself, and said it has introduced additional testing and sanitation measures. No confirmed illnesses have been reported in connection with these recalls.

What listeria does

Listeria can cause fever, muscle aches, vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC. More serious infections can lead to confusion, a stiff neck and seizures. Pregnant people, newborns, older adults and people with weakened immune systems face the highest risk.

If you have one of the affected products, the FDA's advice is straightforward: do not eat it. Throw it away or return it to the place of purchase, and clean any surfaces or containers it touched. If you ate smoked salmon and develop fever, muscle aches or other symptoms, contact a health care provider and mention the possible exposure.
